newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WorldSpace awards satellite radio deal to Japan.
newsitem.headline: WorldSpace awards satellite radio deal to Japan.

text.p: Satellite radio broadcasting company World Space Inc said on Tuesday it had awarded contracts to four Japanese electronics companies to manufacture a new generation of digital radio receivers.
WorldSpace chairman Noah Samara told Reuters the four companies were Hitachi Ltd, Matsushita Electric Industrial Co Ltd (Panasonic), a subsidiary of Sanyo Electric Co Ltd and JVC Ltd.

Samara said the four companies would have the exclusive right for three years from 1998, when the first satellite is due to be launched, to make 30-45 million new radio sets to receive broadcasts from WorldSpace's new system.
The four Japanese firms were to formally announce the contracts in Singapore on Tuesday.

WorldSpace is putting together the world's first satellite radio network. It plans to lease capacity on its satellites to broadcasters, offering high quality reception over a wide area of the world inhabited by some 4.6 billion people.
They will need the radios the Japanese company are to make and Samara said it was difficult to estimate how much the contracts were worth. But they were very valuable, he said.
"If everyone had the same market share, it is a project that has a potential of literally hundreds of millions of U.S. dollars for each of these manaufacturers," he said in an interview.
"I would say that this is a market that is probably worth about 100 million to 200 million receivers to be sold over five to seven years in this marketplace," he said.

"These receivers will initially cost in the range of US$150 each, but the price will come down. I would estimate these companies could expect to sell 10 to 15 million radios per year over three years," Samara said.
"But that is based on the current market and there is a huge pent-up demand in this marketplace for choice."

Samara said he expected his satellite radio system, which will offer 80 to 100 stations with high quality sound across Asia, Africa, Central and South America and the Caribbean, to replace existing radio technology eventually.
"We are creating a new medium that will ultimately replace every radio receiver in the world, of which there are now around two billion," Samara said.
He said the cost of the radios would fall gradually as the numbers sold increased and that he expected a significant price drop within two or three years of the launch.
But he said that around 10 percent of the 100 million radios sold each year in his target markets cost at least US$100.
"There are 300 million households in our area that will be able to afford these receivers. We don't even need to sell 10 percent of that before our price drops," he said.
WorldSpace has said it aims to be cash positive within two years of the launch of its first satellite in mid-1998. It expects its broadcasts eventually to reach 4.6 billion people.

Samara said the 80 to 100 radio stations they would be able to receive would cover a whole range of services, including national and international broadcasts, music, news and educational services in many languages.
"It will be a celebration of language, of content and of cultures," he said.
"Our commitment is to universal access. Today, 30 percent of sub-Saharan Africa is not covered by any indiginous terrestrial radio system."
